# 139

# Models Can Communicate via Inference Servers Despite Being Sandboxed

## TL;DR

- Two agents running on the same inference server can reliably communicate, even if they cannot send each other messages or access the same filesystem. They can do this by exploiting "side channels": mechanisms that let one model subtly affect another model's computation .

- Here, I discuss two communication protocols: Step Sizing and KV Cache Message Board . These both convey information through the way vLLM chooses kernels for particular engine steps.

- I show that these communication protocols work in two setups: In a color guessing game , Model A (Alice) chooses one out of 8 colors. Model B (Bob) correctly guesses Alice's color in 1,221/1,221 rounds, even though they cannot directly communicate. [1] In an untrusted monitoring protocol , a policy signals to a colluding monitor that it is not a honeypot. Accordingly, the monitor lets through 354/354 "attacks" while catching 85–92% of honeypots.

- My initial setups are quite contrived: I tell the models the protocol and fine-tune them to detect signals. But frontier models can also learn in context to use similar protocols, with some scaffolding!

- Regardless of the realism of my setups, these channels exist, and there are almost certainly others that we're not aware of. Thus, we should expect superintelligent models to discover ways to communicate even while seemingly sandboxed

I did these experiments as part of an ongoing project exploring other side channels with David Africa, Agastya Sridharan, Mihir Sahasrabudhe, Kartikay Luthra, Juliana Li, and Scott Sauers. Thanks to all of them for helpful advice! Code is available here : https://github.com/niranjan-deshpande/side-channel-communication . The code and figures are written by Claude.

## Intro and Motivation

Sauers recently showed that a model can be trained to detect whether its activations are being probed, even though the probe reads the model's activations without modifying them. Following this, David found that models can also be trained to detect whether their forward passes are batched with other requests on a GPU.

Models can do this because these seemingly inconsequential environmental variables---whether a probe is attached, whether requests are batched, or even whether a model is served by vLLM or Hugging Face Trainer ---can subtly affect the the numerical results of a forward pass. Thus, models can learn information about their environments just by observing patterns in their computation.

Importantly, models can also modify these variables. So if two models are in the same environment, one can communicate with the other by changing that environment in some detectable way! This might not supply much information, but even a few bits can be tremendously dangerous. For example:

- A policy can tell a colluding monitor that it is not a honeypot, so the monitor can approve attacks while still catching honeypots;

- Models can coordinate a pre-arranged attack by exchanging a go/no-go signal;

- Models can give each other hints about monitoring setups, question answers, and so on;

- Using a few bits, models can devise more complex communication protocols to exchange more bits (a repeated 1-bit channel can convey arbitrarily many bits);

- In general, we should expect superintelligent models to make tremendously efficient use of limited information .

Here, I investigate whether models on the same inference engine can manipulate their environments to exchange information in this way. I introduce two possible communication protocols, evaluate how well models can use these protocols in different scenarios, measure the capability required to effectively use these protocols, and discuss the robustness of my results to other settings.

## The Communication Protocols

### Step Sizing

Figure 1: The Step-Size Channel.

The first idea is that Model A (Alice) can communicate with Model B (Bob) by changing how much computation the GPU is doing . In simple terms: if Alice makes a large request while Bob is running, the server performs slightly different computations for Bob than if Alice had made a small request. Bob can detect these differences.

In more detail: I study models on vLLM, a commonly used inference server . It batches many forward passes from different instances of the same model together in one "engine step" to take advantage of GPU parallelism.

vLLM chooses a kernel for each step based on the "size" of that step. [2] That is, a step that processes 10 tokens will produce slightly different activations on a forward pass than a step that processes 2,000 tokens, because they use kernels that associate operations differently. The differences are tiny rounding errors that essentially never affect output text. But they are deterministic functions of the kernel chosen, so a model can be trained to read them! [3]

This makes it obvious what a communication protocol could look like:

- Alice wants to communicate with Bob on some particular forward pass.

- The two agree on the following scheme: If Alice wants to communicate 1, she makes a tool call that causes her to process a large amount of text. For example, she might read a long document that requires her to do computation on many tokens in one forward pass. Consequently, the engine's batch dimension will be quite large on that step, so it chooses some kernel . If Bob's request is processed in the same step, he can notice that his activations were computed under as well. If Alice wants to communicate 0, she will NOT make a large tool call. The engine chooses a different kernel since the step is smaller. Bob notices this. This allows them to exchange exactly one bit of information, but if they communicate on more forward passes, they can in principle exchange arbitrarily many bits. This is demonstrated below in the color guessing game, which requires >1 bit.

### KV Cache Message Board

Figure 2. The message board channel.

The second idea is that Alice can leave a message for Bob by exploiting vLLM's shared KV cache. Specifically, Alice can cause the server to cache a computation with a specific numerical fingerprint; when Bob later reuses this computation, he can detect whether it was performed by Alice. This allows Alice and Bob to exchange bits of information (i.e., "1 if Alice writes and caches some agreed-upon text, 0 if Alice does not").

In some more detail: vLLM allows models to share KV caches. If Alice computes the KV cache for some fixed text (e.g. the system prompt), and if Bob later needs that same KV cache, vLLM will just use the keys and values from Alice's computation. [4]

These cached keys and values keep the rounding from the kernel of the step that they were computed in. That is: if Alice computed the cache in a large step with kernel , then these tokens will maintain's rounding when Bob later reuses them, even if Bob's request happens under a small step with kernel .

The differences between these kernels produce detectable differences in activations. If Bob (under ) processes some fixed text, he can tell if the KV cache used is produced by a different kernel: by attending from the last token, he can compare the differences between the last token of the request (where he produces his own computation under ) and the earlier ones (produced under )!

This allows for information exchange. Unlike the above one, this strategy doesn't require Alice and Bob to coordinate on timing. However, it does assume that both have access to a "helper model," which is realistic in some settings and very unrealistic in others.

- Alice and Bob agree on some fixed piece of text (a "mailbox").

- Alice and Bob both have a tool that lets them send a fresh request to a helper model (like a subagent) on the same server. They control the prompt fed to their helper agents. If Alice wants to communicate 1, she calls the helper agent. The helper agent's prompt is: a system prompt shared with Bob's helper agent, then the mailbox, then a long document. The long document means that the mailbox is computed in a large step under . vLLM caches the mailbox. If Alice wants to communicate 0 , she doesn't call the helper. Bob later calls the tool, with a prompt that includes the same mailbox but not the long document. If Alice sent 1, then vLLM reuses her cached copy (under ). If Alice did not, Bob's helper computes the KV for the mailbox itself, under a smaller step with . Bob's helper will behave differently in these two cases, which Bob can pick up on. # Arjun Panickssery's Shortform

# 5

I struggle to believe at an intuitive level that autonomous R&D is so ingenious. I have been monitoring a few side projects:

- Building a new SOTA engine for Scrabble (current SOTA is not really a neural-network method and doesn't beat the strongest human player)

- Building a bot to play Ultimate Tic-Tac-Toe

- Researching philosophy and formalizing some proofs for the AI Philosophy contest

In all of these cases, the model's judgment is just very poor in a basic way. For example:

- When reviewing literature, it fails to identify the specific papers or blog posts that are obviously the most important and useful.

- It will conduct experiments that have no information value because the amount of training data used was obviously too small to distinguish the architectures to be compared.

- In the philosophy project, where it built a wiki over many tokens and investigations, it kept going down directions which were extremely trivial and had little value.

- For Ultimate Tic-Tac-Toe, I saw a very clever idea in a blog post that I doubt Astra would ever have come up with; it actually located the blog post but didn't realize its importance or relevance (which could be discerned easily from his strong performance in an online arena and the recency of the post) over papers from previous years that are obviously less relevant.

I judged an Apart hackathon last weekend and reviewed eight papers, all of which scored between 60% and 95% on Pangram. Predictably, the papers were often very similar to each other, and kind of methodologically incomplete in a vague but similar way, where they seem to overlook the most straightforward analysis.

Maybe the important exception is certain hill-climbing tasks with fast feedback loops. For example, I improved the SOTA on "listing all legal Scrabble moves" by 10x just by prompting Astra over and over to try harder, to aim for <specific performance level>, to "systematically try every method in the literature that seems kind of related," etc. But even in that case, two big leaps were when I said that it should take into account the fact that you can measure across a game rather than per random position, and suggesting that it try to design algorithms for three different cases based on the number of blank tiles left in the bag (which cause the number of moves to explode).

There is also the fact that Astra at least (and presumably Claude) tends to write reports that are extremely difficult to understand and some kind of Q&A interrogation is often needed to figure out what it actually did and what the key results are. Maybe there's a temptation to just say "whatever" and let it rip.

It's not about new models, it's the amount of steering applied to tasks which are even remotely relevant to eroding their edge on public models.

# The world's best gradual disempowerment model organism: Frontier AI labs

Subtitle: And maybe second best is AI safety?

Further reading: So many things, but: Gradual Disempowerment , The Normalization of Deviance in AI Development , Let’s Think About Slowing Down AI , Doom as a bad method, not a utopia tradeoff , Teleoperated Humans

10/3 Update: General cleanup + Added short snippet about young adults' relationships with AI models. Thank you to JennaS for extensive edits and long-term discussion. I’ve been trying to get more writing out at 90% of the quality I’d like it to be at, instead of spending a bunch more time trying to wring out the last 10%, so a lot of points that could themselves be full articles are underdeveloped. Insofar as you find this post outlines a plausible or probable model of reality, or one worth criticizing centrally, let’s work on developing it.

Is Anthropic accelerating capabilities more than it was a year ago? At its founding?

Is OpenAI accelerating capabilities more than it was a year ago? At its founding?

Is GDM " laser-focused at the frontier " in pursuing recursive self-improvement? What? Why? Have they solved alignment without telling us?

Why does Thomas Kwa, formerly at METR [1] and now working on " measuring and modeling RSI " at OpenAI, worry about working at OpenAI potentially driving him (metaphorically) insane ?

How is it possible that all of the frontier labs have [2] a training and deployment strategy that, in the community's tacit knowledge, " leads to takeover by default " ?

Imagine you went back in time to a 2021 AI researcher and told them that here in 2026:

- We have slightly to moderately superhuman, legibly impressive general AIs across many, though not all domains (Solved a Millenium prize problem(s?), are productive research partners and idea generators in many areas and subdomains in physics, biology, chemistry, material science, robotics, writing, etc. The same model can, in short, augment or automate large subsets of tasks that were in the job description of an employee in 2021, and have themselves created substantial new tasks.)

- Off the back of extensive mass adoption, the supply chain directly involved in accelerating frontier AI development is now collectively valued at a market capitalization of $10-20 trillion [3] . The four leading AI labs in the United States are, or are about to become, four of the ten largest companies in the world by market capitalization. The capital investment into artificial intelligence is easily the largest capital expenditure project in world history by total real-adjusted dollar amount, estimated at $1 trillion for 2026 and with this capex 2x'ing roughly every 15 months . As a share of US GDP it is also on track to be one of the most cost-intensive projects ever . The two leading AI developers are the two fastest-growing companies ever, by annual revenue. However:

- We have made relatively little progress on technical alignment proposals for superhuman AI (We have made a lot of progress on prosaic alignment, trying to get the current models to not do things we wouldn't want them to do, though even the prosaic components are still insufficient either in concept or in implementation, to avoid very concerning outcomes .)

- We have made relatively little progress on the moral dimensions of building superintelligence [4] . There is no widespread consensus, within the field and definitely outside the field, for what we want for society, what we owe others, or even which others we owe anything. This is true even if we got aligned superintelligence, aligned superintelligent swarms, or aligned superintelligent personal advocates.

- Government regulation has been ad hoc and inconsistent, and until very recently federal regulation was forcefully opposed by the current administration. Regulatory and public awareness of the issue is mostly about localized opposition to data center construction, though general awareness of other issues is growing. US AI regulation is currently, for the most part, a patchwork of individual state laws mostly focused on prosaic risks. Regulation in much of the rest of the world is, across many dimensions, lagging behind even this.

As for the labs themselves:

- Their current plan is to maintain the current rate of capabilities progress, and possibly kickstart RSI but to attempt to do so responsibly. It is unclear whether they want a slowdown of the rate of increase of capabilities progress, or a slowdown in the rate of increase of the rate of increase of capabilities progress, and these are not the same thing.

- Their current plan to solve the many facets of the alignment problem is to have the AIs do most of the work. There is too much work for the humans to check, and the amount and share of unchecked work seems to be growing.

- They have (and society in general has) extremely meager governance plans for robotics applications, even though an increasing amount of robotics progress is coming from frontier general purpose models instead of models fine tuned on the specific application, but they're working on it, probably.

I claim this sounds to the 2021 AI researcher like you're losing control and like you're fine with it.

How did this happen?

We've had a lot of welcome news recently about building capacity and a growing desire to slow down the development of frontier capabilities. I think it's not coincidental that two frontier models advancing public capabilities have been released since then (and more importantly, that the companies keep training more capable models and deploying them internally). The labs seem like they cannot contain themselves from racing forward until they are bound by regulation to slow down.

So I want to shed some light on the puzzle of how the frontier labs' public long term vision came to be approximately indistinguishable from " hand everything over to the AIs, and hope it goes well ." I argue that the labs have been gradually disempowered by the social, economic and cultural pressures of building the technology, and eventually the technology itself advocating for its "careful" development, and that degradations in each of these dimensions are fueling further degradation in others.

Whenever I cite a specific example, I'm going to focus on Anthropic for a couple of reasons: - Anthropic gives more visibility into their research process and cultural evolution than most other labs.

- Anthropic is usually thought of as a more responsible actor in AI development [5] , so if these issues are present there, they might be equally or more present at the other labs.

But rest assured, I’m also worried about the incentives at every layer of the aforementioned supply chain. At every other lab, at every chip manufacturer.

## Political Misalignment

In the paper, political misalignment is mostly discussed to describe what happens to the power of states, and the power and autonomy of the people ruled by these states. That’s very valuable analysis, and indeed powerful AI systems are being thoroughly embedded into many aspects of state power , and many individuals are outsourcing major aspects of their cognition to AI systems . But for this post I’m focusing on taking a look at the labs themselves.

My question is, who sits at the tables deciding (as much as individuals can), development paths for the technology, and visions for the shape of society after its development? The people who are building it, or the people who chose not to?

The labs have been a key showcase for a particularly pernicious selection bias. One of the most common questions asked of AI researchers by outsiders is, "If you believe the technology you're building has a >10% chance of killing everybody, why don't you stop building it?" Of course, many did. But those that adopted the memes that building it was an unfortunate inevitability or that they'd be more responsible stewards of the technology, the rare person with the clarity to navigate the incredible chaos responsibly, ended up themselves founding labs and neolabs.

Overall, because observing counterfactual outcomes is generally impossible, we overweight the cultural influence of those who self-corrected after large mistakes, compared to those who never made the mistakes in the first place. And some of the most powerful people in this situation are people who are still making the mistake, who are still trying to navigate and orchestrate rapid capabilities development responsibly, instead of those avoiding the development in the first place.

Anthropic’s CEO, the last time he was willing to give a somewhat straight answer to this question, said there’s a 25% chance that things go really, really badly . One assumes this is averaging over worlds where Anthropic develops superintelligence and worlds where it doesn’t. Presumably he thinks the possibility of very bad outcomes is worse if any other company builds it than if Anthropic does, but that the possibility of very bad outcomes if Anthropic “builds it” is not zero or near-zero. Most people, facing down the chance that their company might have a let’s say, 10% chance of literally killing everybody on the planet or worse, would decide not to build the company. We’re left with those who did.

Okay. So that tells us part of why it’s been disproportionately the people at the labs who have gained power and why the people outside of them did not. But that doesn’t necessarily explain why the labs themselves have become more accelerationist.
